Resolution No. 117, Series 2026 - A Resolution Approving an Agreement with the Humane Society of Boulder Valley for Animal Impound Services in the Amounts of $14,200 for 2027 and $14,700 for 2028
children.desc:
The Humane Society of Boulder Valley and the City of Louisville Police Department seek to renew their agreement for animal impoundment and sheltering services. The new two-year agreement would become effective January 1, 2027, and continue through December 31, 2028. The City of Louisville and the Humane Society of Boulder Valley have entered into previous service agreements, with the current agreement expiring December 31, 2026.

The Humane Society of Boulder Valley maintains an animal shelter facility within Boulder County, CO and acts as the receiving agent for animal impoundments, to provide shelter and care for animals brought to their facility by authorized City of Louisville personnel, such as police officers or code enforcement. As per the agreement, the Humane Society is responsible for sheltering and caring for the animals brought to their facility while reasonable efforts are made to locate owners of impounded animal(s) so the animals may be reclaimed. The Humane Society shall hold all impounded animals for a 5-day holding period while working to have impounded animals reclaimed. After the expiration of the 5-day holding period, the Humane Society may evaluate the disposition of any animal not reclaimed by its owner. 

The Humane Society provides 24 hours per day, seven days per week access to its facilities for authorized personnel for the purpose of receiving impounded animals. Exceptions to this access, with reasonable notice to the City, are outlined in the agreement and include emergency situations, legal or regulatory requirements, and unforeseen operational constraints.

This Agreement may be terminated by either Party, with or without cause, provided that termination shall not be effective until 90 days after the terminating Party provides written notice of termination to the other Party.

children.name: Resolution No. 118, Series 2026 — A Resolution Approving an Amendment to the Intergovernmental Agreement to Establish a Collective Special Weapons and Tactics Team (SWAT) and Authorizing an Annual Payment of $1,500 per Assigned Officer
children.desc:
The Louisville Police Department and Boulder County Sheriff's Office entered into an Intergovernmental Agreement in 2006 to establish a regional special weapons and tactics team (SWAT) to consolidate resources and create the capability to respond to the most critical public safety emergency events within the City of Louisville and Boulder County. Combining resources and capabilities is a cost-effective means for smaller police agencies to create capacity to safely and adequately address incidents requiring SWAT intervention and support. The Louisville Police Department maintains its partnership with the Boulder County SWAT team and currently provides one SWAT operator and two Crisis Negotiators to the team. Officers participate on the SWAT team as a collateral duty assignment and all assigned officers have a primary assignment at the Louisville Police Department. Basic police equipment, salary, and overtime costs for these participants are included in the City's budget processes and remain an expense covered by the City of Louisville. 

In early 2026, the Boulder County Sheriff's Office notified the participating agencies that the County would be seeking an amendment to the original agreement asking agencies to help cover administrative fees. They provided a cost breakdown and determined an annual administrative cost of $1,500 would be charged to the home agency for each of their assigned officer(s). This fee would apply to the Tactical Operations team and not to officers assigned to the Crisis Negotiations group. The fees will be paid to the Boulder County Sheriff's office to help cover administrative costs for equipping, training, and managing the team. 

Approval of this amendment would set current costs for the Louisville Police Department at $1,500 per year per tactical operator beginning in 2027. In future years, the department may add one or two additional officers to the Tactical Operations team, but would not likely increase the number of assigned personnel significantly beyond that.

Staff is asking Council to endorse a formal Resident Artist Program at the Louisville Center for the Arts (LCA) that replaces three informal space-use contracts with a defined, application-based program.

The program creates three tiers of grant-awarded participation: Resident Arts Groups, Resident Artists and Emerging Artists. Together the tiers dedicate over 60% of the available time at the LCA to program participants, so the building is used for art and artists in practice as well as in name. The program also adds in-kind support, discounted hourly booking and a way to measure the return on the City's investment.

Resolution No. 120, Series 2026 — A Resolution Approving a License, Improvement and Assistance Agreement with the Downtown Business Association (DBA) for the 2027-2028 Street Faire Season, Including Financial Support of Up to $92,000 per Season
This will be the only reading of this item and final action may be taken. There will be one round of public comment.
children.desc:
The Downtown Business Association (DBA) has produced the Louisville Street Faire for more than 20 years, and the City has supported it through license agreements since at least 2003. Until 2016, the event was largely volunteer-run. In November 2015, Council began providing financial assistance, which has since included police services, funding for the support of a contracted General Manager, and dedicated funds for band support, in addition to numerous in-kind support offerings. 

The proposed agreement covers the 2027 and 2028 seasons and is designed to flex around Front & Center construction, which may make the Steinbaugh site unavailable in 2028. It provides $65,000 per year for the General Manager, $25,000 per year for musical performers, up to $2,000 for 2027 tent installation, police support, fee waivers, and promotion. It eliminates the profit and loss sharing structure. The DBA may instead request supplemental funding from Council if needed, similar to the process the Ice Rink used this year.

1st Reading includes the Staff Presentation and questions from Council. There is no opportunity for public comment. The Public Hearing (2nd Reading) will be set on this item for a later date. The Public Hearing will allow 2 rounds of public comment.
children.desc:
Boards and Commissions (B/Cs) are a vital part of Louisville's governance structure, and an area where additional clarity would be appreciated by all parties. The purpose of this project is to provide that clarity through combining documents into one centralized resource. 

The Board and Commission Handbook (the "handbook") will cover advisory and quasi-judicial boards including the Board of Adjustment, Building Code Board of Appeals, Cultural Advisory Board, Historic Preservation Commission, Historical Museum Advisory Board, Library Board of Trustees, Local Licensing Authority, Open Space Advisory Board, Parks & Public Landscaping Advisory Board, Planning Commission, Recreation Advisory Board, Sustainability Advisory Board, and Youth Advisory Board. The Louisville Revitalization Commission is the City's Urban Renewal Authority and will continue to operate separately.

Complimentary to the handbook is the need to update the City's Municipal Code to implement the various changes discussed and supported by Council at the April 14, 2026, October 6, 2026, and October 20, 2026 Council meetings.

children.name: 832 McKinley Avenue Probable Cause Request
children.desc:
A request to find probable cause to allow for funding of a Historic Structure Assessment (HSA) at 832 McKinley Avenue.

VICINITY MAP:


 

SUMMARY:

The applicant requests finding probable cause for landmark designation to allow for funding of a Historic Structure Assessment (HSA) for 832 McKinley Street. 


Prior to any structure being declared a landmark pursuant to Chapter 15.36 of the Louisville Municipal Code or the establishment of a related conservation easement, or approval of grants for preserving, restoring, rehabilitating, or protecting a landmark property, the property will undergo a Historic Structure Assessment (HSA). Under Resolution No. 102, 2025, a property may be eligible for reimbursement for a historic structure assessment (HSA) from the Historic Preservation Fund (HPF) if the Historic Preservation Commission finds there is probable cause to believe the building may be eligible for landmarking under the criteria in Section 15.36.050 of the Louisville Municipal Code. The purpose of the Historic Structure Assessment (HSA) is to develop a preservation plan to establish priorities for the maintenance of the property prior to any structure being declared a landmark.

children.name: 181 Roosevelt Avenue Demolition Application
children.desc:
VICINITY MAP: 


SUMMARY
The applicant is requesting approval to demolish the existing single family home, garage, and detached guesthouse at 181 Roosevelt Avenue. As the structure was constructed prior to 1955, the demolition review must be reviewed by the Historic Preservation Commission as per Louisville Municipal Code (LMC) Section 15.36.020. The applicant intends to rebuild the home on the property without preserving or rehabilitating any potentially historic aspects of the existing home. 

Louisville Municipal Code (LMC) Section 15.36.020 defines demolition as an act that removes fifty percent or more of the roof area as measured from directly above, fifty percent or more of the exterior walls of a building as measured contiguously around the building, or alteration on any exterior wall facing a street. The purpose of demolition reviews, according to Section 15.36.200, is as follows:


The purpose of the review of permit applications for demolition, moving, and removal of buildings constructed in or before 1955 is to prevent the loss of buildings that may have historical or architectural significance. The purpose of this chapter is also to provide the time necessary to initiate designation as an individual landmark or to consider alternatives for the building.


Under Section 15.36.200 of the LMC, if the commission finds that the building may have historical significance under the criteria, the commission may place a stay on the demolition and, “no permit for demolition, moving or removal shall be issued for a period not to exceed 180 days from the date the permit application was accepted.” In addition, Section 15.36.200 states, “The commission will make all reasonable efforts to expedite resolution of the application or request.” 


HISTORICAL BACKGROUND:

Information from Gigi Yang, Louisville Historical Museum


The history of 181 Roosevelt is notable for its unique evolution as a property on the rural edge of Louisville city limits and proximity to several early mines. Central to its history is the unresolved date of construction and the fire that destroyed what is considered to be the original home. Peter and Leah Blankette sued the Public Service Co. for damages and their case set precedents for future Colorado lawsuits. The property also contributes to the immigration story of English, Italian, and French families in Louisville and illustrates the lifestyle of coal-mining families into the mid-20th century.

Early Ownership
Johnson’s 1st Addition was platted in 1890 by Mahlon V. Johnson. It was the second residential subdivision to be platted, after the Jefferson Place Addition was platted in 1880. The earliest known deed for Lot 15, Block 1, is to Lawrence W. Spangler who purchased the land from the Ajax Coal Mining Co. in 1893 for $65. Not much is known about Lawrence Spangler other than that he was in the Louisville area between 1893 and 1906. The Ajax Mine operated for a short time from 1889-1892, and it is unclear whether the house on this property was originally part of the Ajax Mine or was built or moved in later. In 1897, Lawrence Spangler sold the property to Joseph H. Fearn and it is assumed that Fearn lived here, making the likeliest date of construction for the house to be between 1892-1897. John Blake purchased the property from Joseph Stengel in 1905 and owned it for almost twenty years, however very little is known about him. 

The Fire and Peter and Leah Blankette (Blanketti) 1923-1952
Peter and Leah Blankette (Blanketti) owned the property between 1923-1952. In March of 1928, the Blankette house caught on fire during a windstorm and burned down. The report of the fire in the Rocky Mountain Daily describes a “six-room house…at the edge of Louisville.” This description implies that there was an original, larger house on the property and that the current house was not identified as 181 Roosevelt until after 1928. The Drumm’s Wall Maps from 1909 and 1925 both show two structures on this lot and it is not known which structure was the principal family home that burned down. No additional records, photos, or floorplans were discovered that show what the original buildings may have looked like. In December of 1928, Peter and Leah Blankette filed a lawsuit against the Public Service Company of Colorado claiming that the destruction of their home was due to faulty wiring that caused the fire. During these years, the Blankettes no longer had a house and the 1930 census shows them living at either the Monarch Coal Camp #2 or Coalton Camp. Peter continued working at the local mines and likely moved into company housing. 

Boulder County’s current online records give 1892 as the house’s date of construction. However, the date offered by the County could not be verified by other documents, including the 1948 County Assessor card which does not list any date of construction but does show the house on the property with the address of 341 Roosevelt. As was sometimes done, the date of construction may have been copied from other houses in the neighborhood which were constructed roughly between 1892-1915. The style of the house is in keeping with other miner’s homes in Louisville during this time period. It is worth considering whether the current house at 181 Roosevelt was moved from one of the mine camps since the design of the current building is a traditional style for miner’s housing and it may have been more economical for the Blankettes to purchase and move an older house than to rebuild or build a new house. However, both the 1909 and 1925 Drumm’s map show two buildings on the property and it is also possible that the current house was the second building that was already on the lot, potentially left from the Ajax mine era. A building from the Ajax Mine, being one of the earliest mines, could explain the assigned 1892 date of construction for a building left on the property.

Recent Ownership
Several other families lived at the home after the Blankette's with limited social significance. From 1977 to 1983, the house was used as a rental property or left vacant. In 1980, Louisville City Council annexed the parcel to the City of Louisville and changed the house number from 341 Roosevelt to 181 Roosevelt to align with other properties on the same block. Joslin sold 181 Roosevelt to William and Elizabeth Keane in 1983. The Keanes lived at this address until 1988 when they sold it to George Campbell who lived there until 2010. 

In 2010, David & Jeanette Bangs became the current owners of 181 Roosevelt.

PROS Guidebook Adoption
      This will be the only reading of this item and final action may be taken. There will be one round of
      public comment.
children.desc:
Staff are seeking City Council’s adoption of the PROS Guidebook which contains both the Long Range Plan (LRP) and Trail System Plan (TSP).


Adoption would be the culmination of 28 months of planning, development and community engagement. The effort began with collecting feedback on the plan’s Request for Proposal (RFP) from Council and the PROS Advisory Boards. Consultant procurement then involved interviews with shortlisted firms and a Council presentation to refine the preferred consultant’s scope prior to contract authorization. Throughout the planning process, staff and consultants gathered valuable input on the broader community’s needs, desires, and priorities via the following engagements:

  • 10 PROS Advisory Board presentations/discussions spread across the four PROS Advisory Boards 
  • 7 staff-led pop-up community events, each at Division-specific locations 
  • 3 formal Council meeting presentations/updates for direction (not including RFP review or adoption or the budget allocation approvals)
  • 3 stakeholder group interviews with 18 individuals of varying interests 
  • 2 public open houses with over 250 total participants 
  • 1 half-day trails workshop with 25 diverse attendees 
  • 1 open-link public survey with 1,407 responses 
  • 1 resident-only, statistically valid survey with 766 responses
  • 1 additional 35-day publicly promoted feedback window to seek feedback on the final draft versions of the Guidebook via Engage Louisville 

Guidebook adoption is put forth via two separate resolutions – one for the LRP and one for the TSP. While both plans are part of the overall PROS Guidebook, the Long Range Plan sets a strategic direction for four PROS divisions (Parks, Recreation & Senior Services, Open Space, and Coal Creek Golf Course), whereas the Trail System Plan focuses on the future of the City’s shared pathway system and serves as a standalone planning document.


Since the presentation of both draft plans at the August 25th City Council meeting, staff and consultants have worked to incorporate Council feedback along with public input received during the final engagement window. At a high level, these refinements included: further copy-editing, streamlining plan terminology, better conveying the flow of the planning process, polishing plan maps and graphics, and refining the Action Plan Matrix to illustrate priorities and anticipated implementation timeline estimates. 


Staff recommend adopting the Guidebook resolutions to begin the new two-year budget cycle with renewed clarity on the PROS Department’s purpose and strategic direction for serving Louisville’s residents in the years to come.

children.name: Resolution No. 95, Series 2026 — A Resolution Approving a Business Assistance Agreement with Arsenal Health LLC in the Amount of $208,400 for an Economic Development Project in the City of Louisville
children.desc:
Arsenal Health LLC is an integrated health optimization company looking to locate at 600 S. Pierce Avenue in Louisville. The business operates multiple locations in Colorado and Arizona and is looking to open a corporate headquarters and flagship health optimization center in Louisville in 2026.

The proposed location is estimated to generate between $4.3 million and $5.0 million in sales over the first seven years of operation at the Louisville location. The project represents an estimated $1.5 million in tenant improvements with additional investments in medical and laboratory equipment as the company continues to expand. 

The business anticipates having 15 employees at opening and 29 employees after three years. The average salary is anticipated to be around $80,000 with variable benefits. 

Staff is proposing an incentive of 50% of the eligible generated sales tax for five years, up to $200,000 (two hundred thousand dollars). In addition, staff is recommending a rebate of half of the building permit and sign permit fees with a not-to-exceed of $8,400 (eight-thousand and four hundred dollars).

children.name: Resolution No. 96, Series 2026 — A Resolution Approving an Enhanced Business Assistance Agreement with Infleqtion Quantum, LLC in the Amount of $281,114 for an Economic Development Project in the City of Louisville
children.desc:
The City of Louisville provides new and expanding businesses incentive assistance through the Business Assistance Program (BAP). This program allows for rebates of building permit fees, consumer use tax and sales tax. Previous amendments to the program have also allowed for vacancy bonuses, enhanced assistance and small business support. The BAP program is regularly evaluated for effectiveness and needs to continue to support new and expanding businesses. 

The BAP application notes that Infleqtion Quantum is considering an expansion of office and lab space to accommodate growth related to recent contracts.  The expansion is anticipated to retrofit existing office space into a quantum lab space that includes quantum systems, precision optics and photonic systems, software and controls, research and development space, and engineering and testing space. 

Staff is proposing an incentive for Infleqtion Quantum with a not-to-exceed amount of $281,114.25.

children.desc: Fire Smart Louisville, a voluntary, neighborhood-focused wildfire risk reduction initiative, began in early 2026 in response to the Wildfire & Conflagration Risk Assessment (WCRA). The program seeks to empower residents through education, expert guidance, and financial incentives, while coordinating resources across the City of Louisville, the Louisville Fire Protection District (LFPD), Boulder County, and partner organizations. Early accomplishments show strong community interest and demonstrated effectiveness. Fire Smart Louisville submitted a proposal for a scope of work for 2027 which recommended expanding and institutionalizing the program through funding a $100,000 contract with the Boulder Watershed Collective, enabling mitigation activities in high-risk neighborhoods and continued public outreach.

The reservations support potential electric vehicle (EV) charging installations at seven City-owned locations, including four facilities currently included in the City's Capital Improvement Program (CIP) and three additional locations being evaluated in partnership with Boulder County.

Approval of this resolution is limited to acceptance of the rebate reservations. It does not approve final charger locations, equipment purchases, construction, consultant contracts, or additional City expenditures. 

Staff will return to Council for subsequent approvals, including final project locations, implementation plans, funding agreements, and contracts, as applicable.

Sales and Use Tax Collection Report – August 2026

Audit Revenue: Audit tax collections in August 2026 totaled $190,619. This revenue figure includes $40,678 in penalties and interest assessed on delinquent sales tax payments. YTD Audit revenue total for 2026 of $2,405,775.

Sales Tax: Increased MoM (August 2026 vs August 2025) by 20.9% for a total amount collected of $2,185,837. In-city businesses generated $1,056,243, an increase of $112,841 or 12%. Outside city businesses generated $1,129,594, an increase of $265,453 or 30.7%.

Cumulative Performance: YTD 2026 sales tax revenues exceed our budget by $1,700,105 or 11.1%. Compared to last year, sales tax revenue increased by $1,970,020 or 13.1%. All tax revenues combined YTD 2026, including sales tax, use, building, auto, lodging, bag taxes, and audit total $23,064,975. Removing audit, it is $20,659,200.

Consumer Use Tax: Consumer use tax collections for August 2026 amounted to $162,805, reflecting purchases brought into the city without the corresponding sales tax. Use tax remains an unstable revenue base due to its inherent unpredictability.

BAP Refund: Due to a significant BAP agreement, three new lines have been added to the Revenue History Report for tracking and reporting purposes.
